1016.title: Infinite spaces
1016.hook: Pascal: the eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me
1016.howItsDone: Readers of Pascal's Pensées, Christian and otherwise, return to his fragments on the infinite spaces and the thinking reed when they think about the human place in a vast universe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the frog and the pond, and your line was the sound of water. Did a tap or a kettle stop you for a breath? Today a new stretch of this block begins, with philosophers, poets and scientists, starting with a French thinker who looked at the night sky and admitted it scared him. Day one thousand sixteen.

Away from the city lights, on a clear night, the sky stops being a ceiling. It opens. The stars aren't painted on anything. They're out there, at distances you can't hold in your head, and between them is dark, and the dark goes on. Some people feel wonder at that. Some feel a cold drop in the stomach. Most of this block has been about the first feeling. Today is about the second, and it comes from Blaise Pascal, a French thinker who wrote it down in one short line.
screen: `THE SKY STOPS BEING A CEILING.` → `WONDER, OR A COLD DROP.` → `BLAISE PASCAL.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In his Pensées, a word that means thoughts, Pascal writes, in Trotter's translation: "The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me." Not delights. Frightens. It's an honest place for awe to begin. The sky doesn't answer. It doesn't even notice. Second, where we stand. Elsewhere in the same book, Pascal asks what a human being is in nature, and answers with a riddle: nothing compared to the infinite, everything compared to nothing, somewhere in the middle between the two. Too small beside the infinite, too large to be nothing. Stuck in the middle, and looking out. Third, the reed. Then Pascal writes, again in Trotter's words: "Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed." A vapor, a drop of water, he goes on, could kill us. And yet if the universe crushed us, we would still be nobler than the thing that killed us, because we know we die, and the universe knows nothing of it. Fourth, who's frightened. Readers disagree about whose voice the frightened line is. Some hear Pascal himself, a man of Christian faith, being honest about his fear. Others hear him speaking in the voice of a doubter he hoped to reach. Either way, look at the shape of it. The silent spaces are vast, and they know nothing. The small, frightened one under them is the only one in the picture who knows anything at all.
screen: `ETERNAL SILENCE. INFINITE SPACES.` · `NOTHING, EVERYTHING, AND THE MIDDLE.` · `A THINKING REED.` · `THE UNIVERSE KNOWS NOTHING OF IT.` · then, large: `THE SILENT SPACES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to look at the night and feel small. If it's dark, go to a window or outside and look up. If it's daytime, save this for tonight, or close your eyes and recall the darkest, clearest sky you've seen. Let your gaze go past the nearest star to the dark behind it, and past that. Let yourself feel the size of it, even if it's uncomfortable. Then notice the one doing the looking: breathing, small, aware. Hold both together. If you pray, you can bring the silence and the fear as they are. The bell holds the time.
Infinite spaces. Pascal's line: the eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me. Awe with its cold side showing. Today's word.
Your line: the silent spaces. Tonight, before bed, look out at the dark for one minute, and remember Pascal's thinking reed. Day one thousand sixteen.

Pascal calls a human being a thinking reed

readers all agree the frightened voice is Pascal's own

options: the universe, because it's bigger.
the human, because they know they die.

fork.reveal: we would still be nobler than what kills us, because we know we die, and the universe knows nothing of it.

what it means: awe with its cold side showing, and a small, aware human under a sky that knows nothing.
what a scholar hears: readers debate whether the frightened voice is Pascal's own or a doubter's he meant to reach.

1017.title: Two things
1017.hook: Kant: the starry heavens above and the moral law within fill the mind with awe
1017.howItsDone: Readers of Kant often meet this passage on its own, and some people who keep a reflective practice pair a look at the night sky with an evening review of their own conduct.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascal at night, and the silence of the infinite spaces that frightened him. Your line was the silent spaces. Did you look at the night sky? Today a second philosopher looks at the same sky and finds a second thing to set beside it. Day one thousand seventeen.

Two directions. Up, where the stars are. And in, where a sense of duty says: this must be done. Immanuel Kant spent a whole book on duty and reason, argued step by careful step. It's not light reading. Then, in its conclusion, he stops arguing and writes something closer to a confession. Two things, he says, fill the mind with admiration and awe, and the feeling keeps growing the more often and the more steadily we think about them. The starry heavens above. And the moral law within. That pair is today's lesson.
screen: `UP, WHERE THE STARS ARE.` → `IN, WHERE DUTY SPEAKS.` → `TWO THINGS.`

segments.voice: First, notice the pairing. Stars are an easy thing to stand in awe of. Kant puts something beside them that doesn't shine at all: the sense, inside a person, that some things must be done and some must not, whatever they cost. For him the two belong together. He says he doesn't have to hunt for either one as if it were hidden in darkness. He sees them both in front of him, and ties them straight to the awareness of his own existence. Second, the sky. Kant says the view of a countless crowd of worlds seems to wipe out his importance, as a creature of matter who must give that matter back to the planet he stands on. Yesterday, Pascal felt that smallness as fear. Kant names it plainly and doesn't look away. Third, the law within. Here the arithmetic flips. The same person who shrinks under the stars, Kant says, is raised up by the moral law, given a worth that doesn't depend on size, or on the body, or on the world of things. Fourth, the growing. A view seen every day can wear thin. Kant claims the opposite for these two: the oftener and the more steadily you reflect, the more they fill the mind. Some readers hear in that a description of a practice, not just a feeling. Looking up, and looking in, every day, and finding they don't wear out.
screen: `TWO THINGS: ABOVE AND WITHIN` · `THE STARS MAKE A PERSON SMALL` · `THE LAW WITHIN MAKES A PERSON LARGE` · `AWE THAT GROWS WITH LOOKING` · then, large: `ABOVE AND WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice comes in two halves: look up, then look in. If you can, step to a window or outside. For the first minute, look up. Sky, ceiling, clouds, whatever is above you. Let it be bigger than you are, and let yourself be small under it. After about a minute, close your eyes and turn the same attention inward. Is there one thing you already know is right to do? A call owed, a truth to tell, a kindness put off. Don't argue with it. Just look at it, the way you looked at the sky. The bell holds the time.
Two things. Kant's pair: the starry heavens above, the moral law within, and the awe that grows the longer you look at them. Today's word.
Your line: above and within. Once today, when you step outside, glance up for a few seconds. Then, before sleep, ask what the law within asked of you today. Day one thousand seventeen.

what it means: Kant sets the night sky and the moral law side by side, and finds awe in both.
what a scholar hears: in the passage the sky shrinks a person's importance while the law within raises a person's worth, so one awe makes us small and the other makes us large.

1018.title: A presence
1018.hook: Wordsworth felt a presence that disturbed him with joy
1018.tomorrow: A world in a grain of sand
1018.howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path keep a habit of slow walks outdoors, and readers of Wordsworth often return to this passage from Tintern Abbey as a way of naming moments of awe in nature.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kant's two things: the starry heavens and the law within. Your line was above and within. Did you look up last night, and then look in? Today a poet walks back into a valley and meets something he can't quite name. Day one thousand eighteen.

"Five years have past; five summers, with the length of five long winters!" That's how the poem opens. William Wordsworth is back on the banks of the river Wye, a few miles above Tintern Abbey, looking at a landscape he last saw five years before. Same cliffs. Same quiet. Same smoke rising from the trees. But he isn't the same, and the poem is about the difference. Partway through, he tries to say what this place has given him. And what comes out isn't a view at all. It's a presence.
screen: `FIVE YEARS HAVE PAST.` → `THE SAME VALLEY.` → `A DIFFERENT MAN.`

segments.voice: Here are his words: "And I have felt a presence that disturbs me with the joy of elevated thoughts; a sense sublime of something far more deeply interfused, whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, and the round ocean and the living air, and the blue sky, and in the mind of man". Four things to notice. First, the odd verb. The presence disturbs him, and what it disturbs him with is joy. Not calm. Not comfort. A joy strong enough to unsettle. Kant yesterday spoke of admiration and awe; Wordsworth adds that awe can shake a person, even when it's glad. Second, interfused. The presence isn't standing somewhere outside the world, looking in. It's mixed through things, the way light is mixed through air. Third, the address list. Where does this something live? In the light of setting suns, the round ocean, the living air, the blue sky. Ordinary things, things anyone can see on a clear evening. Fourth, the last stop on the list: the mind of man. The same presence that lives in the sunset lives in the one who is watching it. And notice what Wordsworth never does in these lines. He doesn't give it a name. He says presence. He says something. Some readers hear God in it; some hear nature; some hear both. The poem leaves it unnamed, and seems to want it that way.
screen: `A JOY THAT DISTURBS` · `SOMETHING DEEPLY INTERFUSED` · `SUNSETS, OCEAN, AIR, SKY` · `AND IN THE MIND` · then, large: `A PRESENCE.`

segments.voice: The practice is to walk slowly outdoors. If you can't go out, walk slowly across a room, or stand at an open window. Take steps at half your normal speed. Don't look for anything in particular. Let the light, the air and the sky do what they do. If a moment comes that stirs you a little, let it. If nothing comes, that's part of it too. Just keep the slow pace, and keep the senses open. The bell holds the time.
A presence. Wordsworth's name for something he couldn't name, living in sunsets, ocean, air and sky, and in the mind that sees them. Today's word.
Your line: a presence. Once today, at a window or outside, look at the light for ten seconds and ask what else is there. Day one thousand eighteen.

screen: `DAY 1018 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A WORLD IN A GRAIN OF SAND.`

1019.title: A world in a grain of sand
1019.word: A world in a grain of sand
1019.hook: Blake: see a world in a grain of sand
1019.howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path practice close looking at one small object, a seed, a stone, a grain, as a short daily meditation, and Blake's opening lines are often read alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wordsworth's presence, living in sunsets and sky and the mind that sees them. Your line was a presence. Did you catch the light for ten seconds? Today the awe shrinks down to something you could lose under a fingernail. Day one thousand nineteen.

Pour a little salt onto a dark table. Each grain is tiny and rough-edged, and it is easy never to give one a second look. The last few days have been about big things: infinite spaces, the starry heavens, the round ocean. Today a poet points the other way. William Blake begins a poem not with the sky but with the smallest thing on a beach, and says the whole world is in it. Not a picture of the world. The world.
screen: `A LITTLE SALT ON A DARK TABLE.` → `FROM THE STARS TO A GRAIN.` → `THE WORLD IS IN IT.`

segments.voice: Here are the opening lines of Blake's poem Auguries of Innocence: "To see a World in a Grain of Sand and a Heaven in a Wild Flower, Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand and Eternity in an hour." Four pairs, each one small beside large. First, a world in a grain. Notice the verb: to see. Blake isn't making a claim about sand. He's describing a way of looking, close enough and long enough that the small thing opens. Second, a heaven in a wild flower. Not a garden rose. A wild one, the kind nobody planted and nobody waters. Third, infinity in your hand, eternity in an hour. The biggest things there are, set inside a palm and a single hour. Some readers hear this as a promise that the ordinary day is big enough. Fourth, and this part is easy to miss: the poem keeps going. After those four lines comes a long run of couplets, and many of them aren't about beauty at all. They're about harm, to caged birds, starved dogs, hunted hares, and to people too. The very first: "A Robin Red breast in a Cage puts all Heaven in a Rage." The same seeing that finds heaven in a flower finds heaven's anger at a caged bird. If a grain holds a world, then a small cruelty isn't small either. Blake's way of seeing cuts both ways. The tiny thing is holy, and so the tiny wrong matters.
screen: `A WORLD IN A GRAIN` · `A HEAVEN IN A WILD FLOWER` · `INFINITY IN YOUR HAND` · `SMALL THINGS MATTER BOTH WAYS` · then, large: `A WORLD IN A GRAIN.`

segments.voice: The practice is to look closely at one grain or seed. Find one now: a grain of rice, of salt, of sand, a seed from a piece of fruit, a crumb of soil. Put it on your palm, or on something dark. For two minutes, look only at it. Its edges. Its color. Whether it catches light. When the mind wanders off, bring it back to the grain. You don't have to see a world. Just keep looking, and see what the looking does. The bell holds the time.
A world in a grain of sand. Blake's way of seeing, where the smallest thing holds the largest, and where small harms matter too. Today's word.
screen: `A WORLD IN A GRAIN OF SAND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a world in a grain. Today, pick one small thing you'd usually rush past, a crumb, a coin, a leaf, and give it five full seconds. Day one thousand nineteen.

1020.title: Charged with grandeur
1020.hook: Hopkins: the world is charged with the grandeur of God
1020.howItsDone: Christians who love poetry often read God's Grandeur as a prayer of praise, and people on a personal spiritual path use its images of shaken foil and deep-down freshness as a prompt for noticing beauty in worn, everyday places.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Blake's grain of sand, with a world inside it. Your line was a world in a grain. What small thing did you give five seconds to? Today a poet says the whole world is about to flash. Day one thousand twenty.

Take a sheet of kitchen foil, hold it near a window, and give it a shake. For a split second it throws light everywhere, then goes dull again. Gerard Manley Hopkins used that exact picture, shaken foil, in a short poem about God and the world. He was a Christian poet and a Jesuit priest, and his poem names God in its first line and the Holy Ghost in its closing lines. Between them, he says the world is like that foil. Shake it, and it flashes. It's charged.
screen: `SHAKEN FOIL, FLASHING.` → `GOD IN THE FIRST LINE.` → `THE WORLD IS CHARGED.`

segments.voice: The poem is God's Grandeur, and it opens: "The world is charged with the grandeur of God. It will flame out, like shining from shook foil". First, charged. A charged thing is loaded, full, ready to go off, like a storm cloud before lightning. Hopkins doesn't say the world has grandeur sitting in it quietly. He says it's packed in, waiting to break out. Second, two ways it breaks out. It flames out, sudden, like the foil. And it "gathers to a greatness, like the ooze of oil crushed": slow and heavy, the way oil seeps out of something pressed. Grandeur that flashes, and grandeur that seeps. Third, the honest middle. Hopkins doesn't pretend the world is all shining. "Generations have trod, have trod, have trod; and all is seared with trade; bleared, smeared with toil". The soil is bare, and feet in shoes, he says, can't even feel it anymore. Fourth, the turn. "And for all this, nature is never spent; there lives the dearest freshness deep down things". Not on the surface. Deep down. And the poem closes with its reason: "Because the Holy Ghost over the bent world broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings." For Hopkins, the freshness has a source, and he names it, in the language of his Christian faith. Some readers who don't share that faith still come back to the first two images: a world that flashes, and a world that seeps.
screen: `CHARGED: LOADED, READY TO FLASH` · `FLAME OUT, OOZE OF OIL` · `SEARED WITH TRADE` · `FRESHNESS DEEP DOWN THINGS` · then, large: `CHARGED.`

segments.voice: The practice is to notice one flash of beauty. Look around wherever you are, slowly, for anything that catches the light: a glass, a screen's edge, a leaf, a drop of water, someone's hair. When you find one, stay with it. Watch how the light moves on it when you move your head a little. If nothing flashes, look for the slow kind instead, something quietly lovely that's been there all along. If you pray, you can let the poem's first line be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Charged with grandeur. Hopkins's picture of a world full of God's grandeur, ready to flame out like shaken foil, and fresh deep down even when worn. Today's word.
Your line: charged. When a worn, ordinary corner of your day suddenly catches the light, let the word come back to you. Day one thousand twenty.

screen: `DAY 1020 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE JOURNEYWORK OF THE STARS.`

1021.title: The journeywork of the stars
1021.hook: Whitman: a leaf of grass is no less than the journeywork of the stars
1021.howItsDone: Readers of Whitman often return to Song of Myself on walks outdoors, and some people on a personal spiritual path use his lists of small creatures as a prompt to look at ordinary living things as finished, careful work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hopkins and a world charged with grandeur, ready to flame out like shaken foil. Your line was charged. Did anything flash at you? Today, a single blade of grass. Day one thousand twenty-one.

A child runs up with two fistfuls of grass and asks: what is it? That's a scene from Walt Whitman's Song of Myself, and here's how the poet tells it: "A child said What is the grass? fetching it to me with full hands; how could I answer the child? I do not know what it is any more than he." A grown man, stumped by a handful of grass. The poem circles that question for a while. And later in the same poem, he gives an answer you wouldn't find in any botany book.
screen: `WHAT IS THE GRASS?` → `I DO NOT KNOW.` → `AN ANSWER LATER ON.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "I believe a leaf of grass is no less than the journey-work of the stars, and the pismire is equally perfect, and a grain of sand, and the egg of the wren". First, no less than. Whitman isn't saying grass is a little bit wonderful. He's saying it's equal to the stars' own work. Not a step down. Journeywork is an old craft word for work done by a trained hand. So in Whitman's picture, a single blade is something the stars made, and made well. Second, the list keeps going. The pismire, an old word for an ant, is "equally perfect". So is a grain of sand, which we met two days ago with Blake, and the egg of the wren. Whitman piles them up so nothing gets ranked lower. Third, the next line: "And the tree-toad is a chef-d'oeuvre for the highest". Chef-d'oeuvre is French for masterpiece. A tree-toad, a masterpiece fit for the highest. And then, "the running blackberry would adorn the parlors of heaven". A bramble from a ditch, good enough for heaven's living room. Fourth, notice the first two words: I believe. Whitman doesn't claim to have measured this. He states it as his belief, the way the child's question got no measured answer. Wonder, for him, starts with admitting he doesn't know what grass is, and ends with refusing to call any of it small.
screen: `NO LESS THAN THE STARS` · `THE ANT IS EQUALLY PERFECT` · `A MASTERPIECE FOR THE HIGHEST` · `I BELIEVE` · then, large: `JOURNEYWORK OF THE STARS.`

segments.voice: The practice is to look at one blade of grass. If there's grass nearby, pick a single blade, or kneel and look at one where it grows. If not, a houseplant leaf, a herb from the kitchen, even a weed in a crack. Look at its edges, its veins, the way it narrows to a point. Turn it in the light. No need to think anything grand. Just look at it as if someone skilled had made it. The bell holds the time.
The journeywork of the stars. Whitman's phrase for a leaf of grass: no less than the stars' finished work, and nothing in his list ranked lower. Today's word.
screen: `THE JOURNEYWORK OF THE STARS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: journeywork of the stars. When you step on grass today, or pass a weed in the sidewalk, let the line come back. Day one thousand twenty-one.

1022.title: The transparent eyeball
1022.hook: Emerson, on a bare common at twilight, feels himself become nothing and see all
1022.howItsDone: Readers of Emerson often meet this passage from Nature as a description of awe outdoors, and some people on a personal spiritual path practice standing still in open spaces, attention turned outward, as a short daily discipline.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Whitman's leaf of grass, no less than the journeywork of the stars. Your line was journeywork of the stars. Did you look at a blade? Today ends the week, with a man crossing a muddy field at dusk. Day one thousand twenty-two.

Snow puddles. A bare town common. Twilight, and a cloudy sky. Nothing special happening. Here's how Ralph Waldo Emerson describes it in his book Nature: "Crossing a bare common, in snow puddles, at twilight, under a clouded sky, without having in my thoughts any occurrence of special good fortune, I have enjoyed a perfect exhilaration. I am glad to the brink of fear." No mountaintop. No good news. Wet feet. And then, a few sentences on, with his thoughts gone to the woods, he reaches for a very strange picture.
screen: `SNOW PUDDLES AT TWILIGHT.` → `NO SPECIAL GOOD FORTUNE.` → `A PERFECT EXHILARATION.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "Standing on the bare ground, my head bathed by the blithe air, and uplifted into infinite space, all mean egotism vanishes. I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all". First, the ordinary setting. Emerson goes out of his way to say nothing lucky had happened. The joy doesn't come from his day going well. It comes from bare ground and open air, the same in the woods as on the common. Second, glad to the brink of fear. It's an edge we've met before this week. Pascal's spaces frightened him. Wordsworth's presence disturbed him with joy. Emerson's gladness comes right up to fear and stops there. Third, what disappears. Not Emerson himself: what vanishes is "mean egotism", the small, grasping self that keeps score. With that gone, he says, "I am nothing; I see all". A transparent eye doesn't look at itself. It only lets the world through. Fourth, look back at the week. Seven people, seven ways of looking. Pascal and the silent spaces. Kant's two things, above and within. Wordsworth's presence. Blake's world in a grain. Hopkins and a world charged. Whitman's grass, the journeywork of the stars. And Emerson, nothing, seeing all. Some of them name God, as Emerson does a few words later, calling himself "part or particle of God". Some leave the name out. Each of them stood still long enough for something to come through.
